moment: A glass slipped off the table and I caught it before I even thought about it.
question: How did I catch it before I even thought about it?
summary: Fast, practised movements run on circuits that don’t wait for conscious thought. Awareness arrives a moment after your hand is already moving.

beats.title: Something moves
beats.text: Light from the falling glass hits your eyes. Within a few tens of milliseconds, signals pass through the thalamus to your visual cortex.

beats.title: Motion detected
beats.text: Your motion area picks up something dropping fast. The posterior parietal cortex works out where it is compared with your hand.

beats.title: Launch
beats.text: Without waiting for you to decide, your motor cortex sends commands down the spinal cord. At the muscles, acetylcholine triggers the contraction, and your hand shoots out.

beats.title: Corrections in flight
beats.text: The cerebellum predicts where the glass will be and adjusts your hand’s path on the fly, faster than you could steer it on purpose.

beats.title: Awareness catches up
beats.text: Around now you consciously notice: glass falling! In lab studies, people start correcting a reach before they become aware of the change they’re reacting to.

beats.title: The jolt
beats.text: Your heart jumps once it’s all over. The alarm system arrived a little late to help, but it will make sure you remember the near-miss.

whyItFelt: It feels like you acted without thinking, and in a sense you did. Quick, well-practised actions are handled by circuits that don’t wait for conscious thought. Awareness is more like a report that arrives after the action has started, which is why the catch feels almost magical.

tryThis.title: Test your own speed
tryThis.text: Try the reaction-time experiment in the Lab. Most people land somewhere between 200 and 300 milliseconds.

tryThis.title: Practice makes it automatic
tryThis.text: Sports drills work because repetition builds fast, automatic routes, so less has to pass through slow, deliberate thinking.

finePrint: Timings are approximate. Reaction speed varies with age, alertness, practice and how expected the event is.
A glass falling from table height takes about 0.4 seconds to hit the floor, so a catch is fast but possible.
